openers.title: Finish My Sentence
openers.prompt: Finish these out loud: "Peanut butter and ___." "Once upon a ___." How did your brain know what comes next?
openers.teacher: The class calls out endings together, then partners explain how they knew. Ask: "If a chatbot guesses the next word the same way, what could go wrong?"
openers.answer: You guessed from patterns you have heard many times. A chatbot also predicts likely next words from patterns, which is why it can sound right and still be wrong.
openers.lookFor: Students say something like "I've heard it a lot" and connect it to a chatbot guessing, not knowing.
openers.next: Next, we will build a paper word-guessing machine and test its guesses.

openers.title: Confident and Wrong?
openers.prompt: A chatbot says: "Lake Marigold in Pinecrest County is the deepest lake on Earth. Scientists agree." Fact or fake, and how would you check?
openers.teacher: Students hold up 1, 2, or 3 fingers, then write one way to check on a whiteboard. Optional: you ask a district-approved chatbot a question on the projector and the class checks its answer against a trusted source. Ask: "Does sounding sure make something true?"
openers.answer: Fake: Lake Marigold and Pinecrest County are made up for this opener. "I need to check" is the smart reflex; chatbots can state invented facts confidently, so we check a trusted source before we believe or repeat it.
openers.lookFor: Students name a specific check (an atlas, a library database, a trusted website) instead of trusting the confident tone.
openers.next: Whenever an AI tool gives you a fact this week, write down where you checked it.

openers.title: Draw Exactly What I Say
openers.prompt: Write three instructions for drawing a smiley face. Your partner is a robot who draws exactly what you say, nothing more.
openers.teacher: Partners sit back to back; one reads instructions and the other draws only what is said. Swap, then ask: "Which words made the robot's drawing match, and which made it go weird?"
openers.lookFor: Students revise a vague step ("draw eyes") into a precise one ("draw two small dots near the top of the circle").
openers.next: Clear instructions help with people and with AI prompts; next we will build a recipe for clear prompts.

openers.title: Password Line-Up
openers.prompt: Sort these practice passwords from weakest to strongest. None of these are anyone's real password.
openers.teacher: Write the five on the board; table groups agree on an order and send one person to rearrange them. Ask: "What makes the last one hard to guess but easy for you to remember?"
openers.answer: Weakest to strongest: 123456, fluffy, Kai2016, PurpleTacoJumpsHigh, Purple-Taco-Jumps-High-7!. Long, silly passphrases with symbols are strong, and names and birth years are easy to guess. Never share your real one, except with a trusted grown-up.
openers.lookFor: Groups explain that length and unexpected words matter more than a single number.
openers.next: Invent a silly practice passphrase (not a real one) and share how you would remember it.

openers.title: Grandma, Teacher, Stranger
openers.prompt: Ravi wants to post: "Home alone till 6! Here's a pic of my front door on Birch Lane." Stand up if you'd be OK with a stranger seeing that post.
openers.teacher: Students stand or stay seated; ask a sitter and a stander to explain. Then ask: "How could Ravi change the post so it's safe to share?"
openers.answer: It shares when he is alone and where he lives. Online posts can be copied and last a long time, so leave out location, schedule, and home details.
openers.lookFor: Students suggest removing the time and street, or posting later without the door photo.
openers.next: Before you post or send anything this week, ask: would I be OK with a stranger seeing it?

openers.title: Ad or Info?
openers.prompt: Sort these into ad, information, or clickbait.
options: "Ms. Okafor's class guide: how to plant bean seeds"
"Try GlowKicks sneakers, the ones all the cool kids wear!"
"You won't BELIEVE what this cat did next!!!"
"This video is sponsored by Snack Galaxy"
openers.teacher: Read each; students use corners of the room (ad, info, clickbait). Ask: "What words gave it away?"
openers.answer: Info: the bean guide and library hours. Ads: GlowKicks and the sponsored video. Clickbait: the cat headline, which uses shocking words to get a click.
openers.lookFor: Students point to clue words like "sponsored," "cool kids," or "won't believe."
openers.next: Spot one ad or sponsored video at home and name the trick it used.

openers.title: The Giant Fish Photo
openers.prompt: A post shows a fish bigger than a boat, caught at Willow Creek Park: "Real photo, taken yesterday!" Before you share it, what are your steps?
openers.teacher: Describe the photo aloud, or show a teacher-made edited image on the projector. Partners write two steps on a whiteboard, and then you ask: "Why is Stop a better first move than staring really hard?"
openers.answer: Stop first, then find better coverage: look for the same story from a trusted source. Photos can be cropped, edited, or made with AI, so staring is not enough.
openers.lookFor: Students list "stop" and "look for other sources" rather than "zoom in to find glitches."
openers.next: Next we will be Photo Detectives and try these moves on more tricky pictures.

openers.title: Credit the Creator
openers.prompt: Jada put a drawing by an artist named Lu Chen on her poster. Rafael used an AI tool to brainstorm his poster's title. What should each of them do?
options: Say who made it or helped
Say they did it all themselves
openers.teacher: Students hold up 1, 2, or 3 fingers. Then pairs write the exact credit line Jada and Rafael could add. Ask: "Why does an honest note matter, even for AI help?"
openers.answer: Say who made it or helped. Jada writes "Drawing by Lu Chen," and Rafael adds "I used AI to brainstorm title ideas and chose my own."
openers.lookFor: Pairs write a specific credit line for both the artist and the AI help.
openers.next: Add a credit line to the next project you turn in.

openers.title: Screen or Chart Paper?
openers.prompt: Your team is making a poster about recycling. Would you rather make slides on devices, or one big chart-paper poster together?
openers.teacher: Students move to one side of the room and each side gives its best reason. Ask: "What does our team need to show, and which tool (or no tool) helps us show it?"
openers.lookFor: Students justify the choice by the job to be done, such as "we need to add photos" or "we all need to work at once."
openers.next: In your next team project, write down which tool you picked and why.

openers.title: Rewrite It Kind
openers.prompt: In a game chat, Nico writes to Sam: "lol your video is so bad." Rewrite it so it's honest, kind, and helpful.
openers.teacher: Students write one rewrite on a sticky note, then read it to a partner. Ask: "What changed, and how would Sam feel now?"
openers.lookFor: Rewrites name something specific and offer a next step, such as "The ending was funny; maybe make the sound louder."
openers.next: Use one honest, kind comment during peer feedback today.

openers.title: My Balance Goal
openers.prompt: Think about your screen time and your green time this week. Write one small goal you can check off by Friday.
openers.teacher: Model one goal ("I'll read outside for ten minutes twice"), then students write theirs on an index card. Ask: "How will you know if you met it?"
openers.lookFor: Goals are small, specific, and include a way to track them.
openers.next: On Friday, check your card and tell a partner what worked.

openers.title: Which File Name Wins?
openers.prompt: You need to find your plant journal next month. Which file name will help you most?
openers.teacher: Students hold up 1–4 fingers. Then pairs invent a naming rule the class could use. Ask: "What should every file name tell you?"
openers.answer: Science-Plant-Journal-Oct, because it tells the subject, topic, and when. Good names help you own and find your work.
openers.lookFor: Pairs create a rule like "subject, topic, date."
openers.next: Rename one file today using our class naming rule.

openers.title: Is the Speaker Always Right?
openers.prompt: Fact or fake: "A smart speaker only turns on when you say its wake word, and its answers are always right."
openers.teacher: Students vote with thumbs up, down, or sideways for partly. Ask: "What should you never say near a speaker, and why?"
openers.answer: Partly true. Speakers listen for a wake word but can mishear and turn on by accident, may keep recordings, and answer by guessing, so keep private info away from them and check important answers.
openers.lookFor: Students name a private detail to keep away from speakers and say answers can be wrong.
openers.next: With a grown-up, check the settings or rules for any talking helper at home.

openers.title: Is a Lime a Fruit?
openers.prompt: A sorting AI learned "fruit is red or yellow" from pictures of apples and bananas. Stand up if you think it will call a lime a fruit.
openers.teacher: Students stand or sit, then two volunteers explain. Ask: "What training pictures would you add to fix the pattern?"
openers.answer: It probably won't, because its pattern only says red or yellow. AI learns from the examples it gets, so missing examples create mistakes and bias.
openers.lookFor: Students suggest adding green, purple, and orange fruit to the training pictures.
openers.next: Look for a rule in math or science today that only works for some examples.

openers.title: Headline From 2040
openers.prompt: Pretend headline from the future: "Robot Helpers Now in Every Classroom in Maple Hollow." What's one good thing and one tricky thing?
openers.teacher: Partners each name one good and one tricky thing, then pair with another pair to compare. Ask: "Did someone notice a problem you missed? What rule would fix it?"
openers.lookFor: Students add an idea from a classmate and propose a rule, such as "a teacher checks what the robot says."
openers.next: We will vote on class rules for a future helper and post the winner.
